At matched target-model accuracy and 250 ms of added round-trip latency, the full system with the router delivers 1.95x and 1.55x the throughput of the same baseline on SPROUT and OlympiadBench, respectively, while sending only 47% and 39% of the queries to the cloud.

title: Context Matters: Improving LLM-Based Code Summarization with Hierarchical Information
author: Alexandre Petrachini
Breno Bernard Nicolau de FranÃ§a
Guido Araujo
abstract: Source code documentation plays an important role in software quality activities, such as code review, program comprehension, maintenance, and bug fixing. However, it is often fragmented across individual code elements and focuses on local implementation details, providing little information about their surrounding context. This limits both developers' understanding of software systems and the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs), whose reasoning is constrained by finite context windows. Enriching documentation with hierarchical context has the potential to improve software comprehension and support downstream, quality-related tasks for both developers and LLM-based tools. In this paper, we present an in silico study that showcases the impact of augmenting context on the generation of code-level documentation, using a variety of LLMs. By varying the function, class, and module hierarchy visible to the LLMs, we assess whether this variation produces a significant difference in the resulting code documentation compared with the existing documentation, which serves as a proxy for developer intent. Our results show that Documentation-Aware prompts with class or module-level context consistently yield summaries that are closest to the original documentation. Adding surrounding documentation yields statistically significant improvements over the baseline across models, with effect sizes ranging from negligible (DeepSeek) through weak (GPT-4o-mini) to medium (Gemini). We restrict the study to this immediate hierarchical context; call-graph traversal and cross-module dependency context fall outside our scope and are left to future work. These findings provide a clear path to improve automated documentation tools and enhance LLMs' ability to reason about codebases for downstream tasks, such as code retrieval.

title: Three Invisible Failure Modes in Speech-Based Age Estimation for Child Safety
author: Christopher M. Stewart
Kelsey Kraus
J. Elliott Casal
Geoffrey L. Brown
abstract: Child safety in AI depends on the accurate identification of minor users. Young children tend to talk rather than type when interacting with AI, so in practice this identification requires predicting age from speech. We evaluated whether three audio-capable large language models can predict a child's age from their speech across five studies using two speech corpora of children under the age of 13. Models classified children as over 13 on 2.5% to 42.5% of audio responses, and every model that answered placed some 5- to 11-year-olds over 18. While measuring these rates, we uncovered three distinct failure modes. A client library silently double-encoded speech samples, leading one model to classify children aged 5 to 10 years old as being in their thirties and forties with hallucinated explanations. A second model's endpoint was replaced by a successor that refused nearly every age-related question and never produced an age. Every model sometimes placed the same speech sample under 13 and over 18 years of age, but a third model went further, giving threshold answers that contradicted its own numeric estimates. None of these failure modes produced a warning, a status code, or a change in output format, so they would all pass standard monitoring. These results demonstrate why child-safety claims about age assurance should be evaluated at the level of the pipeline rather than the model. We describe the reporting practices that would make such failures detectable.

title: NVFP4-MLA: Unified FP4 KV-Cache Storage and Attention Computation for Multi-Head Latent Attention
author: Chao Ni
Qi Zhang
Xiao Wang
Zongfei Jing
Mingyang Hao
Binghan Chen
Kefeng Duan
Yu-Jung Chen
Mengdi Wang
Tijmen Blankevoort
Jun Yang
abstract: Long-context reasoning and agentic workloads make key-value (KV) cache capacity and attention computation the dominant costs of serving frontier large language models. We present NVFP4-MLA, the first design to push both KV-cache storage and attention computation of multi-head latent attention (MLA) to FP4. NVFP4-MLA co-designs the quantization algorithm with the attention kernel and the cache system. Selective residual compensation preserves model accuracy by adding NVFP4 residuals only to the quantization-sensitive channels. Two-dimensional quantization blocks make the shared latent cache compatible with the different reduction directions of the two attention batched matrix multiplications (BMMs), removing requantization between them. On DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi-K3, NVFP4-MLA matches BF16 MLA average accuracy across nine benchmarks while compressing the MLA KV cache by 3.20x and 3.05x relative to BF16 MLA. On NVIDIA Rubin GPUs, NVFP4-MLA speeds up the attention kernel over FP8 MLA by up to 2.82x on DeepSeek-R1 and 2.71x on Kimi-K3, and lowers p90 time to first token in agentic multi-turn serving by up to 3.5x and 2.1x, respectively. In disaggregated DeepSeek-R1 serving, it also raises per-GPU throughput by up to 2.30x.

title: Bilateral Log-Linear Attention
author: Kazi Ashik Islam
Guojing Cong
abstract: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

title: TMA: Sim-to-Real Forceful Humanoid Manipulation via Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation
author: Yiting Chen
Kelin Yu
Sarthak Kaingade
Bryan Trinh
Kaiyu Hang
Roberto Martin-martin
Nima Fazeli
X. Alice Wu
abstract: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.

title: Robot Demonstration Videos Should Include Transparency Disclosures
author: Nozomi Nakajima
abstract: This paper argues that the robotics and AI community should adopt disclosure standards for demonstration videos. As physical and financial constraints limit direct public access to embodied AI, public dissemination of progress in robotics is mainly through curated demonstration videos rather than direct experience with the technology. In a large-scale (N=9,341), pre-registered experiment across six countries, we find that the general public struggles to discern both the visual authenticity (e.g., distinguishing real footage from CGI) and behavioral authenticity (e.g., distinguishing autonomy from teleoperation) of robot demonstration videos. The omission of these details distorts public perception, leading people to overestimate the ability of robots to perform tasks and navigate real world environments. Using evidence from behavioral science, we design a disclosure intervention and demonstrate that the inclusion of clear disclosures in robot demonstration videos significantly improves discernment of visual and behavioral authenticity, as well as understanding robots' capabilities. We propose the adoption of disclosure standards for robot demonstration videos to accurately calibrate public expectations and promote transparency in robotics research.

title: PREFACE: Separating Shared Corrections from Prefix Conditioning in PEFT
author: Novanto Yudistira
One Octadion
abstract: Does input-conditioned parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) improve because it uses the current input, or because it adds a useful learned correction? We investigate this distinction with PREFACE, a bounded channel controller for PEFT-adapted projections that requires no test-time gradients. The controller reads observed context; in multiple-choice likelihood scoring, its state is independent of the candidate continuation. Our central study freezes IA3, tuned LoRA, and DoRA adapters and matches controller architecture, initialization, batches, and updates across current-prefix and learned-global controls. Across ARC-Challenge and SciQ, current-prefix control improves all six mean accuracies over frozen adapters, but none of its paired contrasts with learned-global control excludes zero. Replacing its corrections with their training-prefix mean changes accuracy by at most 0.34 percentage points; input-varying corrections contribute only 1.8-2.8% of correction RMS. On ARC test, frozen-adapter current/global controls score 25.68%/25.77%, distinct from the earlier jointly trained 23.1% to 26.4% gain over IA3. We derive and evaluate static compilation of fixed corrections, separating deployment simplification from statistical equivalence. Broader GPT-2, Pythia, and Qwen experiments show family-, task-, and scoring-dependent gains, with modest recent-model effects. The study provides an intervention-based evaluation of conditional PEFT: improvements over a static adapter do not by themselves demonstrate a benefit from input matching.

title: NEMESIS2.0: LLM-Aided Netlist-Driven Performance Equation Modeling for Accelerated Analog Circuit Sizing
author: Subhadip Ghosh
Ramesh Harjani
Sachin S. Sapatnekar
abstract: This work presents NEMESIS2.0, an open-source LLM-aided framework that automatically derives equation-based performance models for analog circuits. The resulting equations provide fast, accurate surrogates for SPICE evaluation. To validate the method, equation-based models are developed for seven circuit test cases in a commercial 65nm CMOS technology, covering 15 metrics on five operational transconductance amplifier topologies, and six metrics on two dynamic comparator topologies. When tested on 1000 unseen variants of these seven designs, each corresponding to a different set of independently sampled transistor sizes, the accuracy is found to be within 5% of SPICE. To demonstrate use cases for NEMESIS2.0, the generated models are used as performance evaluators in multiple transistor sizers based on different population-based stochastic search optimizers. For each of the seven test cases, transistor sizing is performed for 100 different sets of performance specifications, with final SPICE simulation confirming that 83.3% of the resulting designs meet all specifications after a single sizing run. The rest fail to meet the specifications due to discrepancies between the model and SPICE, and require iterative resizing under tightened specifications; all such scenarios meet specifications within five iterations. Within the transistor sizers, this equation-based performance analysis evaluates ~400 design candidates per second, versus 0.14 candidates per second for SPICE-based evaluation, achieving 196-238x sizing runtime speedup, including final SPICE verification.

title: Revealing the Biases of Large Language Models By Inferring Prior Distributions
author: Joshua Ryo Cheng
Thomas L. Griffiths
Jake C. Snell
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been known to exhibit a wide range of social biases including name-nationality associations, occupation-gender associations and racial stereotypes. Existing approaches to evaluating these biases typically involve measuring surface-level behavior where a model is fed a dataset of prompts and its outputs are scored relative to ground-truth answers. Inspired by prior elicitation in cognitive science, we propose a different perspective that reconstructs latent bias as a prior underlying the model's behavior. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem where, given prompt-response observations on a bias benchmark dataset, we infer a low-dimensional latent distribution that summarizes the model's stereotyping tendencies. This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.

title: Role-Separated Diffusion Transformers: Global Rule Isolation and Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression
author: Zhiguang Liu
Yi Shang
abstract: We present Role-Separated Diffusion Transformers (RoSeDiT), a new diffusion transformer architecture that isolates the global rule from the image tokens. RoSeViT showed in visual reasoning that a vanilla ViT spreads a shared rule over all $L$ tokens at an entropy of order $Ld$, whereas an enforced controller route reduces it to order $d$. In class-conditional DiT and SiT, the class and the noise level are explicitly conditioned by adaLN, so a RoSeViT-style controller channel on the ViT side is insufficient to establish the full role separation. By introducing the adaLN listening mechanism, which makes adaLN compute under the controller's command, RoSeDiT brings the entropy theorem and role separation into the latent diffusion domain. Under the same SiT training and evaluation protocol at the same level of parameter count, RoSeDiT surpasses SiT at all four model scales at 400K steps, and RoSeDiT-L/2 even surpasses SiT-XL/2's 17.2 FID with 15.34 and 32% fewer parameters. RoSeDiT-XL/2 surpasses SiT-XL/2's 7M-step FID of 8.3 at 1.4M steps with 7.98, using one-fifth as many training steps. We further observe that models with the same denoising loss can have a large FID gap, which indicates a misalignment between the denoising objective and the image manifold. We formalize this phenomenon into Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression (DSMC), a two-stage training schedule with which RoSeDiT-XL/2 surpasses SiT + REPA's 4M-step FID of 5.9 at 2.4M steps with 5.84.

title: A PTAS for Euclidean Capacitated Vehicle Routing
author: Zachary Friggstad
Fabrizio Grandoni
Ramin Mousavi
Kinter Ren
Mohammad R. Salavatipour
abstract: In the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), introduced by Dantzig and Ramser in 1959, we are given an $n$-node graph $G=(V,E)$ with metric edges costs $c(e)$, a depot $r\in V$, and an integer vehicle capacity $Q$. The goal is to find a minimum-cost collection of tours, each containing the depot and visiting at most other $Q$ nodes, such that the tours cover all the nodes. In this paper we focus on the Euclidean CVRP problem, where the nodes represent points on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and the edge costs are the respective Euclidean distances. Euclidean CVRP generalizes the classical NP-hard Euclidean TSP problem (the special case with $Q=n-1$), that admits a PTAS [Arora FOCS'96/Mitchell SODA'96]. A long-standing open problem has been generalizing the latter PTAS to Euclidean CVRP. A polynomial-time $(2+\epsilon)$-approximation for this problem follows from the PTAS for Euclidean TSP and the tour-partitioning technique for CVRP [Haimovich, Kan Math. OR'85]. This was the best known until a recent improvement of the approximation factor to slightly below 2 [Friggstad, Grandoni, Mousavi SODA'26]. There have been a series of papers presenting improved QPTASs by Das and Mathieu [SODA'10] (time $n^{\log^{O(1/\epsilon)}n}$), Jayaprakash and Salavatipour [SODA'22] (time $n^{O_{\epsilon}(\log^6 n)}$), and recently Sitters [ArXiV'25] (time $n^{O_{\epsilon}(\log\log n)}$). In this paper, we solve the mentioned long-standing open problem by presenting a PTAS for Euclidean CVRP.

title: Advancing the Calibration-Compute Frontier of LLM Classifiers via Asymmetric Duos
author: Berke Akturk
Ali Can Sahin
Rasit Cem Solatay
Emanuel Sommer
Yawei Li
David RÃ¼gamer
abstract: The importance of reliable uncertainty estimation in large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly pronounced, yet modern models remain poorly calibrated and frequently overconfident. In this study, we address this by proposing an efficient method for LLM classifier calibration using the Asymmetric Duos framework. Our approach combines a strong base model with a smaller sidekick model via logit-space fusion, utilizing global scaling parameters optimized on a validation set. Across diverse benchmarks, this Asymmetric LLM Duo consistently achieves best or second-best performance on expected calibration error and negative log-likelihood, without degrading predictive accuracy. More importantly, these gains are realized at a fraction of the computational cost of more complex baselines, placing our method on the calibration-compute Pareto frontier. We further demonstrate that our method acts orthogonal to various established calibration-aware techniques, meaning it can be easily combined with them to consistently boost their performance. Finally, our analysis of the logit-space behavior illustrates how asymmetric fusion successfully mitigates base model overconfidence. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the benefits of an asymmetric fusion successfully transfer to the language domain, providing a simple, highly cost-efficient approach to improving uncertainty estimation in LLM classifiers.

title: Refinement vs. Replanning: Inference Compute Allocation in Robot Policies
author: Alba Maria Tellez Fernandez
abstract: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.

title: B2G-Agent: An LLM-Based Multi-Agent Tool for End-to-End Building-Grid Interactions
author: Xueyuan Cui
Qian Zhang
Xiaochen Liu
Yi Wang
abstract: Buildings are major electricity consumers and can interact with distribution network dispatch through flexible power scheduling. These interactions require distribution network operators (DNOs) and building energy managers (BEMs) to reconcile their operational constraints and perform complex cross-field computations. The lack of cross-domain expertise and unified computational workflows could lead to inefficient or physically infeasible interactions. To address this bottleneck, we develop an end-to-end large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent tool, B2G-Agent, that bridges DNOs and BEMs. The tool deploys three collaborative agents: a Translator for bidirectional cross-domain semantic mapping via hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); an Actor for automated configuration and execution of joint simulation and optimization through directed acyclic graphs; and a Reviewer for memory-augmented reflective failure diagnosis. This workflow abstracts away cross-field modeling complexities and enables both sides to focus on high-level operational decisions. Comprehensive evaluations across 200 synthesized tasks show that B2G-Agent improves the interaction quality score from 66.71 to 85.57 and increases the task success rate from 38.0% to 69.0% over the baseline while satisfying operational constraints. The open-source tool and interface are available at https://github.com/hkuedl/B2G-Agent.

title: Understanding the Role of Reasoning Data in Pretraining
author: Jianhao Huang
Allan Zhang
Ali Payani
Baharan Mirzasoleiman
abstract: Reasoning data expose models to multi-step reasoning, but reasoning traces may cover only a subset of the available facts. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. These trends persist in a full transformer layer with an MLP, softmax attention, and cross-entropy loss. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.

title: More Context, Mixed Results: Evaluating LLMs for Identifier Recovery and Code Deobfuscation
author: Simon Queyrut
Valerio Schiavoni
Giuseppe Antonio Di Luna
Daniele Cono D'Elia
Leonardo Querzoni
Pascal Felber
abstract: Source code is often obfuscated through identifier renaming, incentivizing reverse engineers to develop techniques for recovering meaningful names. To assess how LLMs compare with these techniques, we evaluate 4 traditional baselines and 3 LLMs (Qwen, OLMo and DeepSeek) on identifier detection and semantic recovery across 51 recent Java projects, 3 obfuscators, and 6 context/retrieval settings. LLMs generally outperform traditional techniques on both tasks, but benefit from different forms of context and settings: agentic retrieval yields the strongest detection results, reaching 91.56% $F_1$, while enclosing-class context generally improves semantic recovery at a higher token cost. Despite these gains, exact recovery peaks at 16.42% overall (under one-hop context) and 32.93% for field names (under repository retrieval), which are the easiest to recover. Class identifiers are the hardest to detect, with a mean detection $F_1$ of 48.48% across models, settings and obfuscators. More context is not always beneficial: larger methods hinder semantic recovery. Beyond identifier renaming, our experiments show that control-flow obfuscation degrades both tasks more than string encryption. Our findings provide useful ad hoc insights for reverse engineers choosing models and context strategies to deobfuscate code snippets.

title: Certify, Then Select: Viability-Aware Runtime Steering of Frozen Diffusion Policies
author: Angelo Moroncelli
Loris Roveda
abstract: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Project page: https://clmoro.github.io/cast.

title: Run, Read Back, Refine: Observation Fidelity in Execution-Grounded EDA Agents
author: Yang Liu
Shiwei Hou
Xiyuan Chen
Sen Yuan
Shao You
Feifan Chen
Wencheng Li
Shuyang Hu
Emma Xia
Xiaojing Lu
Wenchuan Zhang
Hao Wang
Fan Xu
Yanfeng Li
Hongwen Li
Yiming Zhu
abstract: Design engineers lose the most time orchestrating flows and patching the gaps where closed EDA tools refuse to interoperate. We present an execution-grounded LLM agent for PyAether, SKILL, and Tcl that closes a generate-execute-refine loop over unified MCP tools (API retrieval, documentation, sandbox execution) and is already deployed in production EDA flows, with a grounding-gap framework positing that EDA-scripting correctness is bottlenecked by observation fidelity at the L4 (situated) layer, which model scale alone cannot reach. On EDA-Scripting-Bench (449 tasks, three languages, four commercial runtimes), the system reaches 76.5% pooled Pass@1 versus 19.7% (pure LLM): the system-level observation axis spans 56.8 percentage points with the model fixed, exceeding the 23.3-percentage-point backbone range with the harness fixed---two axes answering different questions; observation is an under-invested axis whose returns are measurable and graded.

title: Large Language Models for AI Infrastructure
author: Bolin Shen
Shaoyi Huang
Yushun Dong
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to design, optimize, and operate the infrastructure behind AI training and serving, yet the literature remains fragmented across hardware design, machine learning systems, electronic design automation, and high-performance computing. We present a comprehensive survey of LLM-assisted AI infrastructure across its lifecycle, from accelerator design and kernel engineering to compilation, deployment, operations, data management, and energy optimization. We organize the literature by the primary resource the LLM manages: artifact-centric methods for computational artifacts, operational-centric methods for deployment context and system state, and resource-centric methods for data and energy. These categories span the lifecycle and cover AI-specific concerns such as distributed-training configuration, inference serving, GPU-cluster scheduling, and data loading. Building on this taxonomy, we conduct a cross-study quantitative synthesis of reported results. Because studies adopt heterogeneous benchmarks, baselines, hardware, and metrics, we compare methods only where evaluation conditions permit and align results along common dimensions: functional correctness, execution performance, throughput, resource and energy consumption, operational outcomes, and optimization cost, keeping each result's native metric, baseline, and setting rather than collapsing them into a single score. This comparison reveals where LLM-driven methods yield consistent gains, how reported gains in workload orchestration depend on the evaluation environment, from simulators to real clusters and production, and where evidence is still lacking. Together, the taxonomy, lifecycle perspective, and quantitative evaluation provide an evidence-grounded reference for LLM-driven engineering of AI infrastructure.

title: Policy Optimization With Multiple Verifiers via Pareto Rankings
author: Kai Yamashita
Shohei Taniguchi
Hiroki Furuta
Masahiro Suzuki
Yutaka Matsuo
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models. In tasks such as code generation and instruction following, multiple verifiers evaluate whether a response satisfies different requirements. Their outcomes provide detailed feedback about partial success, yet this feedback is commonly aggregated into a scalar reward for policy optimization. Rewarding only complete success discards distinctions among partial solutions, while counts and weighted sums impose comparisons between responses that satisfy different subsets of requirements. We introduce Partial-Order Likelihood Policy Optimization (POLPO), which learns from the comparisons established by verification without first constructing an aggregate reward. Pareto dominance identifies responses that satisfy additional requirements without losing any already satisfied, while leaving responses with conflicting outcomes incomparable. POLPO extends the listwise likelihood underlying Direct Preference Optimization by maximizing the total probability of all complete rankings consistent with these partial orders. This objective provides supervision from verified improvements even before complete solutions are available, without requiring a prescribed ordering of incomparable responses. Experiments on code generation and instruction following demonstrate improved learning efficiency and higher rates of complete requirement satisfaction compared with scalar-reward training. These results support partial-order likelihood as an effective approach to learning from multiple verifiers.

title: SearchChord: Prompt Preselection and Field Recomposition for One-Step Image Editing
author: Boyang Deng
Yuzhen Lu
abstract: Finding effective prompts and seeds for one-step image editors requires balancing edit fidelity, source preservation, and computational cost. To address this challenge, we explore a large collection of candidate edits, where each candidate is defined by a unique prompt-seed pair, and generate corresponding images on demand. We present SearchChord, a training-free framework that leverages a large pool of such candidates, combining text-based preselection, image verification, and latent-field recomposition. Our ablation studies across pool sizes up to 200 candidates show that a pool of 100 offers a cost-effective operating point. Compared with feeding all 100 candidates into recomposition, TextSim preselects a subset of 10 candidates. Rather than uniform averaging, we incorporate image-verifier scores to weight each candidate during recomposition. Experiments on PIE-Bench and the proposed CropWeed-EditBench reveal a trade-off: candidate selection improves target-text alignment, while recomposition better preserves unmodified source content. The oracle verifier achieves the best performance in both preservation and target-text alignment. Practical verification partially recovers semantic alignment, but recomposition still compromises edit fidelity, including in agricultural image edits. These results motivate text-first preselection and stronger verification to balance preservation, fidelity, and cost. Code and data will be made publicly available.

title: Assume/Guarantee Contracts for the Compositional Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning of Heterogeneous Teams
author: Dominic Klukas
Cyrus Neary
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems for heterogeneous teams require agents to collaborate to complete team tasks while making the best use of diverse agent capabilities. We introduce assume/guarantee contracts for heterogeneous multi-agent systems (AGC-MAS) and Iterative Heterogeneous Assignment for MARL (IHA-MARL). AGC-MAS contracts are compositional objects that encode the assumptions provided to, and the guarantees required of, each subtask contributing to the overall team task. We formulate contracts as tuples that specify a subtask, an automaton, timeout and success-probability requirements, and dispatch behavior. The automaton tracks an agent's high-level progress through the subtask associated with its contract and provides a natural mechanism for synchronization across contracts. Our abstraction enables robust interaction across heterogeneous low-level subtask implementations, allows heterogeneous agents to substitute for one another in satisfying contracts, and supports reuse of previously satisfied contracts in new team contexts. Having defined our theoretical framework, we develop a decomposition algorithm that breaks down a team task into a set of contracts. We then propose an iterative algorithm for task assignment and MARL that alternates between assigning contracts representing subtasks to individual agents, training the assigned agents to satisfy their contracts, and assessing their resulting capabilities to inform the next round of task assignments until the team's success probability meets the desired threshold. Our experimental results demonstrate the versatility of contracts in enabling agent substitution and contract reuse. Across three benchmarks with five seeds each, IHA-MARL achieves observed $100\%$ final evaluation success. In CPU timing pilots, comparable baselines required approximately $7$--$11\times$ more training-loop time.

title: RoboCoEvo: Expanding Robot Capabilities through Agent-Policy Co-Evolution
author: Ran Qi
Yixin Xiao
Dawei Wang
Zhiyuan Li
Jinbang Huang
Xuan Zhao
Yintao Ma
Yangzheng Wu
Tongtong Cao
Yingxue Zhang
abstract: Integrating MLLM-based agents with robotic foundation models has attracted increasing attention as a means of enhancing robotic capabilities. However, the improvement of such integrated systems remains largely decoupled across their agent and model components, with advances in one component not necessarily benefiting the other, substantially limiting the capabilities of the combined system. As both MLLMs and robotic foundation models become increasingly capable, fully realizing their combined potential calls for co-evolution, an iterative process in which improvements in agents and robotic foundation models reinforce one another. We propose RoboCoEvo, a failure-guided co-evolution framework that couples the refinement of the agent's explicit and reusable executable knowledge with parameter learning in robotic foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models. Through a code-as-policy formulation, the agent develops and refines executable failure-detection and recovery programs, generating targeted corrective experience. Post-training consolidates the resulting corrective behaviors into the robotic model's end-to-end policy, improving autonomous task execution. Changes in the updated policy's failure distribution, in turn, guide subsequent revisions to the agent's programs. Experiments on BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin demonstrate sustained improvements in autonomous VLA task performance across successive co-evolution rounds.

title: DynaDFlash: Dynamic Feature Projection for Block Diffusion Speculators
author: Aadi Kulshrestha
Reese Chong
abstract: DFlash trains a parallel draft model on hidden features from its target model. Inspired by the previous work of DFlare that introduced per layer combinations of target hidden states, we test whether context dependent weighting of these states helps improve acceptance length of block diffusion speculators. We trained both a DFlash baseline for the Qwen 3 of block size 16, and a dynamic model that computes gates for each layer to affect the magnitude of hidden features before projection. While mean acceptance length between the dynamic model and the DFlash baseline didn't significantly differ, we notice that the dynamic model excels for drafting in the context of math. In an evaluation of 700 prompts from the MetaMathQA and Orca-Math datasets, the mean accepted length improves by 5%. We also found this lead to a 4.1% higher throughput for a subset of the same dataset in the context of speculative decoding.

title: Beyond Benchmarks: Evaluating Large Language Models and Agentic Patterns for Static Code Analysis Warning Classification
author: Lakmal Deshapriya
Sherlock A. Licorish
Brendon J. Woodford
Grant Dick
abstract: Context: Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools support software verification and validation, reducing the time and cost of code reviews. However, the best SCA tools in the practitioner community generate a high volume of false positives, which developers tend to ignore, leading to genuine warnings being overlooked. Accordingly, studies increasingly adopt Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify and reduce false positives. Existing studies have produced promising results on public datasets, but underperformed on unseen datasets. Moreover, researchers do not leverage the full potential of Agentic patterns in LLMs or incorporate established code quality standards for warning classification. Objectives: This study utilises four manually annotated datasets to evaluate the performance of three contemporary LLMs for SCA warning classification in real-world applications, and incorporates Agentic patterns and established coding standards to enhance models' performance, addressing gaps identified in existing studies. Method: Three LLMs were selected using the LiveCodeBench benchmark, and the Structured Chain-of-Thought (SCoT) prompting technique was used to evaluate these LLMs. Furthermore, we incorporated Agentic patterns, such as Debating and Self-Consistency, to potentially improve performance in SCA warning classification. Results: Our results show that the performance of different LLMs varies with the characteristics of the dataset, ranging from 0.52 to 0.96 F1-Score for the best models. Additionally, the use of Agentic patterns does not improve LLMs' performance in most scenarios. Conclusions: SCA warning classification using LLMs works best only with certain warning types. We recommend evaluating LLMs in real-world applications rather than using publicly available datasets/benchmarks to understand their full utility.

title: Reliable Conditioned Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability via Subsolution Learning on Exact Local Windows
author: Seunghwan Jang
Wei Xiao
abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the maximal safe set and a safety filter for a given obstacle configuration, but it must be re-solved whenever the obstacles change, which a deployed robot cannot afford. Learning a single value function conditioned on the obstacle set removes the re-solve, yet it sharpens the central weakness of learned reachability: one network must now cover a whole family of safety problems, and its approximation error carries no preferred sign, so rare obstacle configurations silently produce false-safe states. To address these challenges, we present a conditioned reachability model designed so that the remaining error falls on the conservative side. Specifically, our method caps the obstacle margin, which makes the value function provably local, in the sense that obstacles farther than a known threshold cannot affect it, so the model reads only a body-frame window, trains on small scenes, and transfers to scenes of any size with millisecond per-scene preparation. Moreover, the output structure builds the value bound into the model. By training with counterexample mining over the finite-dimensional window configuration space, we maximize the claimed safe volume subject to the HJ inequality, so the learned set grows toward the true safe set from the conservative side. Across all tested obstacle settings, ours is the only method that combines recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach training with near-zero rollout collisions. We also extend the method to a 10D quadrotor, again with markedly lower collision rates than the baselines.

title: When the Spec Sheet Lies: Injection Attacks on LLM-Generated Compliance Artifacts
author: Adriana Watson
Marco BÃ¼cheler
Grant Richards
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become used more commonly across a variety of fields, a growing body of research has highlighted particular concerns surrounding model security. Notably, prompt injection attacks, where malicious instructions are inserted into prompts, are particularly simple to implement yet capable of inducing devastating effects on the fidelity of model outputs. While there is substantial research surrounding attack models and their effects on chat-based models, browser add-ons, and coding agents, the impact of these same attacks on industrial LLM-generated artifacts has been left largely unexplored. As LLM-enabled agents are increasingly used to skim and generate industrial documents such as Safety Data Sheets (SDS), Quality Control (QC) documents, and Digital Product Passports (DPP), it remains unclear how adversaries may influence these systems to manipulate generated compliance artifacts. This work aims to address this core inquiry by examining how a variety of prompt injection attacks can compromise LLMs with industrial document generation tasks. The study finds that injection attack success varies significantly across different models. Active falsification injections are most successful under all scenarios, while models tend to be most robust against passively injected override requests.

title: Leaning Over to Reach Far-Away Objects
author: Allen Devaraj
William Xie
Nikolaus Correll
abstract: We study supported reaching to extend a humanoid robot's workspace by bracing against the environment for stabilization using a straightforward yet capable whole-body model predictive control (MPC) approach, exclusively with local sensing and fiducial markers. While typical solutions for whole body humanoid control aim at avoiding or accommodating contact, contact is explicitly required to reach objects placed on surfaces far out of normal reach. We employ sampling-based MPC for whole-body leaning, bracing, reaching, and recovery on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid. The controller runs in real-time at 34 Hz on a laptop, transfers sim-to-real, extends reach by about 50 cm beyond the unbraced standing workspace, and sustains the loaded posture for over four minutes, before pose estimation drifts. The controller reaches the commanded target in 89% of trials and completes the full reach-and-recovery cycle in 81%, across 54 trials spanning six targets and three table heights. We further characterize why such a small real-time sampling budget is sufficient, finding that temporal persistence of sampled actions and exploration scale strongly govern success, while CEM provides the widest operating region over planning rate and model mismatch. These results establish a real-world baseline for online, contact-rich humanoid manipulation. Code, videos, and full hardware details are available at https://h12leaner.github.io/

title: EEGHyena2: Fixation-Inspired Joint Lexical-Grammatical Conditional Random Field for Interpretable EEG-to-Text Decoding
author: Xiaoshan Zhou
Chenlan Liu
abstract: A sentence is built from words that carry lexical meaning and grammatical roles, and brain activity during reading reflects both. Current EEG-to-text decoders, however, let a large language model (LLM) propose and order the words, so fluent output can reflect the LLM's prior more than the recorded EEG. In this study, we asked whether fixation-linked EEG carries lexical and grammatical evidence during natural reading and how a decoder can use such evidence. Fixation-related potential analyses showed that content and function words differ reliably in group-averaged EEG but only weakly in single words. We therefore propose EEGHyena2, a structured decoder in which a bidirectional encoder inspired by StripedHyena 2 feeds a semantic head that ranks a fixed lexicon and a part-of-speech (POS) head that predicts grammatical categories; a joint word-POS conditional random field (CRF) scores a restricted candidate lattice, and a frozen Llama-2 scores the candidates in context. On two natural-reading corpora, ZuCo and ROAMM, it matched the state-of-the-art method on BLEU-1 (21.4 vs 21.3), exceeded it on ROUGE-1 F1 (23.3 vs 20.3), lowered the character error rate on ROAMM (75.3% vs 84.7%) and decoded each recording about 3-10 times faster than LLM candidate search. The CRF learned transitions that mirror English syntax, and the encoder drew local context from its convolutions and distant context from attention. Decoders can thus pool weak word-level EEG evidence across the sentence through explicit lexical and grammatical structure, with the language model adjudicating among candidates rather than generating them, which lowers decoding cost and keeps decisions inspectable.

title: Can Agentic LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code? A Study of OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU and TTG
author: Linus Bantel
Anna-Lena Roth
Tim ThÃ¼ring
Jonas Posner
Dirk PflÃ¼ger
abstract: Task-based programming offers more expressive power than loop-level parallelism, but the runtimes providing it differ widely in API style, maturity, and the amount of public code to learn from. This paper asks how well LLM agents write C++ for four of them: OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU, and TTG. Instead of single one-shot prompts, we use an agentic workflow in which the model edits files, compiles, and runs its kernels until it reproduces a reference output. Five locally hosted open-weight LLM implement seven HPC kernels, including matrix multiplication, Cholesky and LU factorization, in all four frameworks and a serial baseline to verify their understanding of the problem in general. Every kernel is evaluated independently for correctness at each concurrency level, strong scaling, and peak memory. Model capability dominates the outcome: three models produce correct, genuinely task-parallel kernels in 57-82% of the cases, while two models rarely compile their own code and almost never succeed. For the capable models, OpenMP Tasking and HPX are handled most reliably, StarPU is close behind, and TTG trails. The best generated GEMM and factorization kernels match or exceed the multithreaded OpenBLAS/LAPACK reference. However, correctness overstates parallel quality: several "parallel" kernels contain no parallelism at all; and serialized task graphs and unsuitable task granularity remain common.

title: Guiding AI Agents to Generate Conjectures by Encoding How Theorems Build on One Another
author: Hita Kambhamettu
Daniel Krashen
Lyle Ungar
abstract: Recently, LLMs have been making headlines, and headway, in mathematical research. Much of this work focuses on proving existing open conjectures. Deciding what to prove is harder and less studied, because of the lack of a clear criterion for what makes a conjecture worth pursuing. We present a method for conjecture generation that builds on the observation that mathematical theorems build on one another: new theorems can modify the setting or hypotheses of earlier theorems, strengthen their conclusions, or extend their scope. We encode these relationships in a new kind of graph, the Theorem Evolution Graph (TEG), which we instantiate as an online search method for LLM agents. An agent builds a TEG in two steps: (1) identifying relevant theorems from papers found by following citations backward and forward from a seed paper; and (2) comparing those theorems to record how one builds on another. LLM judges and an expert mathematician preferred TEG-generated conjectures over those from an unconstrained baseline. LLM judges favored TEG conjectures for significance, ambition, and insight, and favored baseline conjectures for plausibility. Ablations suggest a benefit from constructing and using a TEG even when the available papers are fixed.

title: Learning inadequacy of Bayesian neural operators for PDE-constrained inference and design
author: Pratyush Kumar Singh
Lianghao Cao
E. Bruce Pitman
Danial Faghihi
abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) underpin predictive modeling across science, engineering and medicine. Their use in digital twins, parameter inference and optimal design requires repeated solutions across parameters and scenarios. For nonlinear, transient and multiphysics systems, these calculations can make numerical simulation prohibitively expensive. Here we introduce the residual-informed Bayesian neural operator (RI-BNO), which learns operator inadequacy using a posteriori error estimates from the governing PDEs and incorporates its correction and uncertainty into Bayesian training and prediction. We establish local error bounds for the residual-informed estimates under stability and smoothness assumptions. We demonstrate RI-BNO on a non-linear reaction-diffusion benchmark with DeepONet and latent-subspace architectures, Markov chain Monte Carlo inference of glioma parameter fields from magnetic resonance imaging, and Monte Carlo risk-averse optimization of three-dimensional thermal breaks in building envelopes under manufacturing uncertainty. Across the evaluated examples, RI-BNO improves agreement with finite element (FE) reference predictions, parameter posteriors and optimized designs while using half as many full nonlinear or transient training simulations as the vanilla Bayesian neural operator (vBNO). For thermal break design, online optimization time decreases from 178 hours with the FE model to 18 minutes with RI-BNO. These results demonstrate the value of explicit inadequacy modeling in neural operators for reliable PDE-based inference and design.

title: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live
author: Jovan Popoca Moran
Eduardo de Avila-Armenta
RaÃºl Alejandro Aquino-Ibarra
Jorge Octavio NicolÃ¡s-DÃ­az
Umberto Leon-Dominguez
abstract: A voice agent that negotiates by phone must answer quickly, understand spoken amounts and cope with a caller who talks over it. We compared three architectures for such an agent, negotiating freight rates in Spanish: two cascades (speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis) orchestrated by Pipecat and by LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live, an OpenAI speech model that listens and speaks without separate stages. A program played the carrier with the same 47 recordings of one speaker for all agents, without the telephone network, in 77 calls per architecture over five negotiation scenarios, and measured latency on the listener's side with a validated instrument. Median latency to the content response was 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit) and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live); the confidence interval of GPT-Live's 171.2 ms advantage over Pipecat includes zero. According to its own timestamps, GPT-Live began to answer 800 ms after the end of the line, close to the 0.8 s published by OpenAI; most of the remaining wait, about 1,367 ms and nearly constant, is the audio's round trip through OpenAI's service. A tool call added 0.9-1.1 s in every architecture, more than any difference between them, and the frameworks' self-reported latency fell short of the listener's wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit). Word error rates were low (6.03, 4.93 and 1.47%), but the error on amounts was 13.01% and 12.61% in the cascades, against 2.86% in GPT-Live. With default settings, Pipecat and LiveKit stopped at almost every backchannel and often took it as the carrier's answer: an "ok" spoken over the agent ended in a registered agreement in 3 of 15 Pipecat calls, 2 of 15 LiveKit calls and no GPT-Live call (descriptive counts, not tested). Latency should therefore be measured on the listener's side, and a cascade needs safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannels.

title: DecoEdit: Beyond Flat Control for 3D-Aware Unified Image Editing
author: Xiaotang Gai
Jinbo Xing
Zijie Meng
Jiayi Yi
Jimin Xiao
Yixuan Qian
Yu Liu
Chaojie Mao
Zuozhu Liu
abstract: While recent advances in multimodal image editing have achieved impressive results, current frameworks remain largely confined to ``flat" 2D controls (e.g., text prompts, bounding boxes, or masks). Precise 3D-aware geometric manipulation -- such as coordinating an object's location, physical scale, and 3D orientation while strictly preserving its fine-grained identity -- remains an elusive challenge, typically suffering from severe detail degradation or requiring expensive per-instance fine-tuning. In this paper, we present DecoEdit, an all-in-one image editing framework that goes beyond flat control by seamlessly integrating 1D textual, 2D spatial, and 3D volumetric inputs under a unified architecture. First, to power this unified model, we establish a data curation pipeline and curate a large-scale dataset, namely DecoDataset, containing 1.6 million samples, encompassing diverse multi-dimensional (1D/2D/3D) tasks and their complex compositions. Furthermore, we establish a comprehensive image editing benchmark named DecoBench to systematically evaluate multi-task editing performance. Finally, to address the fundamental trade-off between complex spatial transformations and identity preservation, we propose a novel decoupled pipeline: DecoEdit factorizes the editing process by utilizing structural guidance from SAM-3D to anchor the target geometry, scale, and spatial orientation, while concurrently leveraging a detail-preservation path to lock in high-fidelity textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DecoEdit achieves state-of-the-art results. Notably, on the challenging 3D spatial pose and orientation control tasks, DecoEdit significantly outperforms leading closed-source models such as Seedream 5.0 in both geometric accuracy and identity consistency.

title: Agent-Guided Process Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
author: Rui Zou
Mengqi Wei
Xin Zhao
Ji-Rong Wen
abstract: Large language models have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning, yet in complex multi-step reasoning, an error at any step may propagate along an incorrect path, and the resulting solution may omit necessary branches. Existing natural-language reflection methods often struggle to locate critical errors precisely, while outcome verification typically checks only whether the available candidate answers satisfy the problem conditions and can therefore overlook necessary branches. To address these limitations, we propose Agent-Guided Process Verification (AGPV) for mathematical self-correction. AGPV decomposes the current solution into an ordered sequence of key claims, verifies them individually while invoking a shared mathematical toolbox when needed, and stops upon detecting the first error. A summarization agent converts the failure evidence into a diagnosis that guides a correction agent to re-derive the subsequent solution from that point; AGPV then adapts the next verification iteration to the revised solution. AGPV also verifies solution completeness. We further prove that AGPV guarantees solution correctness and completeness when key claims provide sufficient coverage and local verification is reliable, provided that all key claims pass verification. The implementation compresses long working contexts and reuses successful tool results within each problem. We evaluate AGPV on five challenging mathematical reasoning datasets with four models from DeepSeek, Qwen, and GPT. AGPV achieves an average accuracy of 63.8%, outperforming the strongest among the representative baselines evaluated (50.3%) by 13.5 percentage points, with higher repair coverage than the programmatic-verification baselines.

title: Beyond Plain MCP: Do Decision Models and Code Mode Make Tool Use Cheaper and Faster?
author: Abhishek Rai
abstract: Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateways manage tool catalogs for language model agents using two primary paradigms: code mode where agents write scripts against tool stubs and decision layers which are cheap routers that preselect tool subsets. Using a controlled harness across 12 servers, up to 1,958 distractor tools, and three open-weight agents including Qwen, Gemma, and Nemotron, we present a preregistered evaluation on a sealed test split to determine when each approach succeeds. Code mode substantially outperforms plain MCP, cutting token usage by 70 to 90 percent while significantly boosting utility. Declaring return-shape hints in code mode stubs is a first-order variable, swinging success by up to 39.5 points for lower-performing agents, an effect larger than adding a router. The central hypothesis that a decision layer in front of code mode beats code mode alone is not confirmed, showing minor, statistically non-significant improvements for weaker agents and a slight cost for the strongest. We publicly release our harness, a finetuned 4B tool selection model, and all evaluation traces to support robust community experimentation on local AI privacy and agent architectures.

title: Empowering Masked Diffusion Models to Self-Correct with Leave-One-Out Transformers
author: Sofian Zalouk
Vincent Counathe
Paul JÃ¼nger
Daniel Cao
Daniel Zlotnick
Kilian Q. Weinberger
Christopher De Sa
abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for language modeling, enabling parallel token generation with competitive performance. Yet standard MDMs suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) inability to revise tokens, and (2) sparse training signal. We revisit hollow transformers, which address both limitations by predicting each token from its surrounding context, independently of the input at that position. We introduce the Leave-One-Out Transformer (LOOT), a more efficient and expressive architecture that advances hollow transformers through two complementary advances. First, we redesign the merging mechanism to enable frequent interaction between left and right contexts, substantially improving predictive performance over prior hollow transformers. Second, we derive a lower-variance estimator of the MDM NELBO that supervises all tokens and improves validation perplexity. Together, these advances yield a competitive standalone diffusion language model capable of effective self-correction during inference. On LM1B, LOOT matches the strongest dense-supervision MDM baseline in validation perplexity. On OpenWebText, LOOT achieves higher MAUVE and better generation quality-diversity tradeoffs than prior remasking methods, using $8\times$ fewer forward evaluations and $3.5\times$ fewer inference FLOPs.

title: Wireless Edge-Assisted Adaptive Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models in Physical AI
author: Fatih Temiz
Melike Erol-Kantarci
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable embodied artificial intelligence (AI) by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Emerging use cases in physical AI are expected to drive the need for efficient inference and communication, as the computational demands of the VLA models pose challenges for real-time control with limited onboard resources. Test-time scaling through latent reasoning allows these models to refine hidden representations without generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, but introduces a trade-off between task success, inference latency, and energy consumption. In this paper, we address the efficient collaborative inference under a realistic communication scenario. We propose a wireless edge-assisted framework for adaptive latent reasoning (WEALR) that augments onboard computation with edge computing. A decision-making agent jointly selects the execution location and latent-reasoning convergence threshold. We formulate this joint adaptation as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). A Lagrangian-constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) approach, namely trust region policy optimization Lagrangian (TRPO-Lag), learns to balance task performance and resource consumption under varying wireless conditions and task requirements. We evaluate the framework using LIBERO manipulation tasks, profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced wireless channels. Experimental results demonstrate that TRPO-Lag achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success rate compared to benchmark CDRL methods.

title: Low-Latency LLM-Based Streaming Multi-Talker ASR with Verifiable Rewards
author: Jing Pan
Ruizhi Li
Ju Lin
Jing Zheng
Florian Metze
abstract: LLM-based architectures offer strong generalization and instruction-following capabilities for streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR), but multi-talker use introduces coupled transcription, attribution, and latency challenges. Our wearable setting requires real-time transcription of a conversation between a near-field device wearer and a far-field partner. Because partial hypotheses are rendered on persistent sides of a dialogue UI, speaker roles cannot be permuted and each speaker tag must precede its turn. These sparse tags are weakly optimized by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while committing to a leading tag can delay the text that follows. We therefore post-train a streaming LLM-based ASR model with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), combining a fixed-role Speaker-Attributed WER (SA-WER) grader with a turn-level onset-delay reward. On an eight-direction multi-talker cohort, SA-WER RL reduces SA-WER from $20.51\%$ for SFT to $13.14\%$. Adding the delay objective reduces onset $p50$ by $65\%$ (from $0.918\,\text{s}$ to $0.320\,\text{s}$) and $p90$ by $44\%$ (from $1.389\,\text{s}$ to $0.780\,\text{s}$) relative to SA-WER-only RL, while achieving $12.70\%$ SA-WER. These results demonstrate that fixed-role recognition quality and streaming responsiveness can be improved jointly.

title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
author: Jieyuan Pei
Xin Yan
Mingwei Xu
Haiyi Zhang
Siyu Zou
Zhangyi Hu
Zhuoxuan Li
Yuguang Yang
Rongjunchen Zhang
Cheng Chi
Hui Xiong
Yan Wang
abstract: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.

title: MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
author: Cheng Siong Chin
abstract: Marine and offshore engineering text is spread across preprints, open-access journals, encyclopedias and institutional documents, and the amount of it is small by pretraining standards. We ask how far a lightweight language model for marine and offshore engineering can be taken with parameter-efficient adaptation on a single workstation-class device. Starting from the 4-billion-parameter OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct, we train two independent LoRA adapters, each updating 33.0 million of 4.06 billion parameters (0.81%). Training took 4 hours 40 minutes for the first adapter and 10 minutes for the second on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The first adapter is trained by next-token prediction on a 61.6-million-token corpus covering ten engineering themes. The corpus was built from 13,879 source documents, of which 7,069 were retained after deduplication and a two-tier keyword filter that removes cross-domain lexical collisions. Its validation loss falls from 2.082 to 1.976 over 1,500 steps. Direct testing showed that this adapter could still drift off topic on a retrieval-grounded ballast-water prompt, so we trained a second adapter on 2,295 question-answer pairs (114 hand-written and 2,181 generated by the base model from corpus passages) with the loss restricted to answer tokens. On 20 held-out prompts scored by hand for accuracy, topicality and specificity (maximum 120), the plain base model, the continuation adapter, the instruction adapter and the instruction adapter with retrieval scored 42, 56, 84 and 88. Absolute accuracy stays low (14 of 40 without retrieval and 20 of 40 with it). We report the full pipeline, two negative results (a reverted keyword fix and an instruction run that overfit within 100 steps), and the limits of the evaluation, which uses one small prompt set, no inter-rater agreement measure and model-generated reference answers.

title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
author: Matthias Jammot
Pembe Gizem Ãzdil
abstract: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

title: Personalized Language Models for One-to-Many Private Communications
author: Zihan Hong
Xue Li
abstract: We study relationship-specific continual reply prediction for one-to-many private communication: a system predicts an author's reply to a recurring contact and updates its personalization state when the actual reply becomes available. We propose TRACE (Temporal Relationship-Aware Communication Evolution), which uses author-level lexical habits, contact-specific wording, and temporal expression estimates to guide a frozen language model, with a feedback-driven policy controlling revision. On 216 test emails from eight Enron users, all four main TRACE configurations achieve higher mean BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore and lower mean Reply Style MSE than Base LLM and Base RAG. Component ablations show mixed effects and do not establish statistically reliable improvements in Reply Style MSE after multiple-comparison correction. More accurate state forecasts and larger revision budgets do not consistently improve reply-level metrics. These exploratory findings expose the challenge of turning evolving relationship-specific expression estimates into useful generation guidance.

title: From zero-target transfer to target-site personalization: multi-source training across fall-detection models
author: Jaeseung Ryu
Jae-Hun Jung
abstract: Video-based fall detection could support timely assistance when a person cannot call for help. Unfamiliar cameras and scarce local labels challenge deployment. We examine whether joint training improves cross-dataset detection and subsequent local training. We analyze 2,697 clips from eight OmniFall datasets and one AI-Hub dataset. Positive clips contain a fall or collapse transition, while negative clips do not. We hold out each dataset in turn, training on the other eight. We evaluate three vision-language models (VLMs), Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL, and three visual baselines, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. We evaluate the stored source model without target data for training or selection. For each label budget, we update a separate copy using labeled clips from the held-out target dataset. We call this target-site personalization. We compare the Source-initialized model with Target-only, which skips source training but uses identical target clips and updates. Across nine targets, source training raises mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from frozen-model values of 0.821 to 0.912 for Qwen, 0.883 to 0.947 for LLaVA, and 0.939 to 0.962 for InternVL. With five target examples per class and 26 updates per run, 95% confidence intervals for the AUROC benefit over Target-only lie above zero for Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. With full-target training, they lie above zero only for Qwen and LLaVA. Separate VLM analyses reveal threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections. The benefit varies by model and label budget.

title: Towards Self-Organizing Channel Coding in 6G-Enabled IoT Networks: Trends, Cognitive Architectures, and Open Challenges
author: M. Moazam Azeem
Adil Raja
Ayaz Ahmad
abstract: The sixth-generation (6G) of wireless communication is designed to facilitate distributed edge intelligence, ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC), and massive machine-type communications (mMTC), all of which have the potential to revolutionize the Internet of Things (IoT). Autonomous vehicles, swarm robotics, XR, and industrial automation are IoT-centric 6G applications with demanding requirements; developing efficient, adaptive, and reliable channel coding methods is crucial to realizing this goal. This study explores the adaptation of various channel coding schemes to distributed IoT scenarios in 6G networks, covering both established and developing schemes, including LDPC, Turbo, Polar, and Fountain codes. We evaluate the relevance of recent developments to decentralized IoT designs, including AIassisted cognitive coding, neural network-based decoding, adaptive and context-aware coding, quantum and reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) coding. We further propose CACADe-6G, a cognitive architecture for adaptive channel coding; our evaluation shows that its principal benefit over simpler adaptive baselines lies in reduced switching overhead and energy consumption, rather than a guaranteed reduction in bit error rate relative to a memoryless threshold comparator. We compare different channel coding schemes with respect to latency, energy, and reliability requirements, and highlight important use cases. Findings from this study reveal current research gaps and identify potential future directions for coding in intelligent, large-scale IoT systems, aiming to guide future research and support the deployment of 6G-enabled IoT technologies.

title: Isolating Perception for Multi-View Planning under Occlusion-Induced Partial Observability
author: Kevin Nguyen
Ceyhun Efe Kayan
Feng Liu
Li Zhang
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are beginning to saturate visual planning benchmarks, yet they fail to resolve depth ambiguity and degrade sharply with problem size under occlusion-induced partial observability (PO). We introduce BW-PO based on the Blocksworld domain, a controlled benchmark that reduces existing VLM planners and formalizers to near-zero performance, and propose VLM-as-perceiver, a paradigm that narrows the VLM's role to local perception while delegating cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation to external solvers. Across model-specific challenging subsets of BW-PO, this raises plan success from 1% to 97% for Gemma-4-31B, 0% to 95% for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 3% to 84% for Gemini-3.1-Pro. Isolating perception in this way separates two bottlenecks that are otherwise entangled: reconciliation under depth ambiguity, and completeness of visual extraction under scene density.

title: Do VLMs Really Look at the Road? A Diagnostic Evaluation for Autonomous Driving
author: Shankar Gangisetty
Muskan Singh
C V Jawahar
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for autonomous driving through question-answering benchmarks, yet high benchmark accuracy does not necessarily reflect visually grounded reasoning. We present a diagnostic evaluation framework that systematically probes whether VLMs base safety-critical driving decisions on visual evidence or instead rely on language priors, answer biases, and dataset regularities. Our benchmark comprises two task categories, Adverse Weather and Junctions \& Intersections, with a nuScenes spatial reasoning extension, and evaluates open-source (general, driving, and spatial-reasoning) VLMs along four diagnostic protocols: image versus no-image evaluation, counterfactual weather sensitivity, linguistic robustness under paraphrasing and negation, and spatial reasoning. All ground-truth labels are derived programmatically from BDD100K and DriveLM annotations, enabling reproducible evaluation without manual labeling. Across all models, we find that competitive overall accuracy conceals systematic failure modes, including strong affirmation bias, limited sensitivity to counterfactual scene changes, near-chance performance on negated questions despite high paraphrase consistency, and confident driving decisions even without visual input. These results demonstrate that current open-source VLMs remain insufficiently grounded for safety-critical autonomous driving and underscore the need for diagnostic evaluation beyond aggregate accuracy.

title: A Unified Control Framework, Mathematical Model, and Five-layer Closed-loop Case Study for Embodied Intelligence Control Systems
author: Yiwei Zhou
Zhongcheng Lei
Xiaoran Dai
Wenshan Hu
Hong Zhou
abstract: Embodied intelligence holds that an agent develops cognition and behavior through real-time body-environment interaction, so its control system must tightly couple perception, decision making, learning, optimization, constraints, and physical execution. This report asks whether a unified framework exists, how its mathematical models unify, and how the framework is realized computably. Four conclusions emerge. (1) No single framework is accepted, but the field converges on a common skeleton: from operational-space and whole-body control to MPC, reinforcement learning, active inference, and diffusion/flow policies, all reduce to constrained sequential decision making on the configuration manifold. (2) Two languages describe it-deterministic optimal control (Euler-Lagrange plus constrained OCP, reduced in real time to a QP) and probabilistic inference (MDP/POMDP plus free-energy minimization)-rigorously bridged by control as inference and KL/path-integral control. (3) Engineering unification is already achieved by constrained optimization; the new frontier is cross-morphology, cross-task shared representation. (4) The hardest gap is provable stability and safety, the entry point for spectral, geometric, differentiable-optimization, and safe-learning methods. A single-link manipulator then runs through all five layers: L4 parses the instruction into a reference, L3 identifies a Koopman lifted linear world model, L2 solves a receding constrained QP, L1 adds torque saturation and a CBF, and L0 is the true nonlinear plant. Closed-loop tracking RMSE is 0.0218 rad with all constraints satisfied and a world-model error near 5 x 10^-6 rad, reported with curves and a 3D animation.

title: Distilling Safety Filters for Filter-free Multi-agent RL
author: Srikar Babu Gadipudi
Somayeh Sojoudi
Claire J. Tomlin
